etymology: Greek iaspis (G2393), Hebrew yashpheh (H3471) — a translucent, often green or clear-crystalline quartz; first of the twelve foundation stones of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19) and the very stone that pictures the glory of God Himself appearing on the throne (Rev 4:3). The ancient iaspis was probably closer to what we today would call diamond or clear quartz — "clear as crystal" — not the opaque red-brown stone modern jewelers call jasper.
biblical_def: Jasper is the first of the twelve precious stones laid as foundations beneath the city wall of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19), and it is also the stone John saw when his vision lifted to the throne of God Himself: "He that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone" (Rev 4:3). The Holy Spirit chose this stone twice as a vehicle for the divine glory — clear, brilliant, refracting light without darkening it — because the God of glory is light, and in Him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). The city wall is built of jasper (Rev 21:18); the foundation begins with jasper; and the One on the throne shines as jasper. Old Testament jasper also appears in the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:20; 39:13) — the last of the twelve stones representing the twelve tribes — and in Eden as one of the stones covering the anointed cherub before his fall (Ezek 28:13). The biblical-theological line runs: jasper covered Eden's covering cherub → jasper crowned the high priest's breastplate (representing the twelve tribes brought before God) → jasper lays the first foundation of the New Jerusalem (representing the twelve apostles and the twelve tribes united in the Lamb's city). The stone moves from a fallen anointed creature through the mediated approach of the priesthood to the unmediated dwelling of God with men. Jasper is the mineral testimony that God's glory is unbroken light — and that He has prepared a city for His people where that light needs no sun or moon, because the Lamb is the light thereof (Rev 21:23).
webster_summary: A precious stone, the first foundation of the New Jerusalem and the appearance of Him who sits on the throne.
webster_full: JASPER, noun. An opaque (the ancients said clear) impure quartz, of red, yellow, brown, green, or rarely blue color, sometimes striped or spotted. The biblical jasper of Rev 4:3 and 21:11 is described as "clear as crystal," suggesting the ancient stone was closer to diamond or clear quartz.

In Scripture, the first of the twelve foundation stones of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19); the eighth (KJV order, twelfth in Hebrew) stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:20); a covering of the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13); the stone whose appearance signified the glory of God on the throne (Rev 4:3).
scriptures: Revelation 21:19
And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, a chalcedony; the fourth, an emerald.
Revelation 4:3
And he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.
Revelation 21:11
Having the glory of God: and her light was like unto a stone most precious, even like a jasper stone, clear as crystal.
Ezekiel 28:13

Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God; every precious stone was thy covering, the sardius, topaz, and the diamond, the beryl, the onyx, and the jasper, the sapphire, the emerald, and the carbuncle, and gold.
corruption_summary: Jasper is corrupted when stripped of its theological function and reduced to mere decoration, or when treated as a magical or healing crystal divorced from the Creator who made it.
corruption_paragraphs: On one side, modernist commentaries treat the foundation stones of Revelation 21 as nothing more than poetic adornment — pretty imagery, but signifying nothing in particular. This empties the text of meaning. The stones are chosen, ordered, and named by the Spirit; each carries weight tied to the high priest's breastplate, the temple, Eden, and the New Covenant people of God. To shrug at the names is to refuse what God Himself underlined twice in canon.

On the other side, New Age and crystal-healing spirituality co-opts biblical stones — jasper, sapphire, amethyst, emerald — and assigns them "vibrational frequencies," chakra alignments, or healing properties divorced from God. The Bible nowhere ascribes power to the stone itself; the stone is a vehicle for God's chosen revelation of His glory and His chosen ordering of His covenant people. Jasper does not heal you. The God whose throne shines like jasper heals — and that healing comes through the Lamb whose wounds purchased it, not through a polished rock.
roots_summary: Greek iaspis (G2393), Hebrew yashpheh (H3471) — a translucent precious stone whose ancient identification was closer to diamond/clear quartz than the modern opaque variety.
roots_lines: Greek iaspis (G2393) — jasper; in Revelation 4:3, 21:11, 21:18-19 a clear crystalline stone reflecting divine glory
Hebrew yashpheh (H3471) — jasper; the last stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:20) representing the twelfth tribe Benjamin
The ancient iaspis was probably a clear or diamond-like stone, NOT the modern opaque variegated jasper sold by jewelers today
Twice chosen for theophany contexts: God's appearance on the throne (Rev 4:3) and the foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19)
usage: When John saw the throne, the One sitting upon it shone like jasper — the brilliance of unmediated divine glory.
Jasper crowns the high priest's breastplate and founds the New Jerusalem: a stone bridging Old Covenant approach and New Covenant indwelling.
Don't buy a jasper bracelet for healing; trust the God who chose jasper to picture the light of His face.

etymology: Greek sappheiros (G4552), Hebrew sappir (H5601) — a deep blue precious stone; the second foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19) and the very stone underfoot when the elders of Israel beheld God on Sinai: "under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone" (Exod 24:10). The biblical sapphire was likely lapis lazuli — opaque deep blue with golden flecks — though the corundum gem we now call sapphire also matches the color.
biblical_def: Sapphire is the second foundation stone of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19) and the stone Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders of Israel saw beneath the feet of the God of Israel on Sinai: "and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness" (Exod 24:10). The deep blue color speaks of heaven itself — and the Holy Spirit chose this stone as the visible boundary between God and man at the giving of the Law, and again as the second course of the eternal city's foundation. The sapphire also appears on the high priest's breastplate as the fifth stone (Exod 28:18; 39:11), and Ezekiel's vision of the throne shows it set in sapphire (Ezek 1:26; 10:1). The theological line runs: at Sinai the elders SAW sapphire beneath God and ate before Him without dying — a covenant meal — but the access was strictly bounded, only Moses could approach further; the high priest carried sapphire on his breast as he interceded once a year in the Holy of Holies; Ezekiel SAW sapphire shaped as a throne when he was carried in vision to the heavenly court; and in the New Jerusalem sapphire becomes a foundation we walk on — no longer the ceiling under which we crouch, but the floor on which the redeemed city stands. The progression is from sapphire-as-distance (Sinai) to sapphire-as-mediator (breastplate) to sapphire-as-throne (Ezekiel) to sapphire-as-foundation (New Jerusalem). The God whose glory once kept Israel at the foot of the mountain has prepared a city whose foundations rest on the very stone that once marked the unapproachable.
webster_summary: A precious blue stone, second foundation of the New Jerusalem and pavement beneath the feet of the God of Israel at Sinai.
webster_full: SAPPHIRE, noun. A precious stone of a fine blue color, next in hardness to the diamond. Biblical sapphire is likely lapis lazuli (deep blue, opaque, gold-flecked) or possibly true corundum sapphire.

In Scripture, the second foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19); the stone seen under the feet of the God of Israel by the elders at Sinai (Exod 24:10); the fifth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18); the appearance of the throne in Ezekiel's vision (Ezek 1:26).
scriptures: Revelation 21:19
And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire.
Exodus 24:10
And they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness.
Ezekiel 1:26

And above the firmament that was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, as the appearance of a sapphire stone: and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it.
Exodus 28:18
And the second row shall be an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond.
corruption_summary: Sapphire is corrupted when its Sinai-grounded covenant context is forgotten and the stone is treated as a generic luxury good, or when modern engagement-ring marketing replaces its theological weight with mere status signaling.
corruption_paragraphs: Reduced to commodity. The stone that paved the floor of heaven under the feet of the God of Israel — the stone that defined the visible boundary between sinful man and holy God at Sinai — is now mostly a luxury good in jewelry-store cases, priced by carat and color saturation. The biblical weight of sapphire as a witness to the unapproachable glory of God is almost entirely lost in the modern consumer association.

On the other side, the modernist commentary tradition dismisses the Exodus 24:10 vision as primitive theophany imagery — as if Israel's elders just imagined what was overhead — rather than treating the text as actual revelation that the God of glory permitted seventy-four covenant representatives to SEE the floor of heaven and to eat and drink in His presence. The text is far more startling than either treatment allows: real men, real God, real meal, real sapphire under His feet. Strip either side of this — the historicity or the typological weight — and the New Jerusalem's sapphire foundation loses its echo.
roots_summary: Greek sappheiros (G4552), Hebrew sappir (H5601) — a deep blue precious stone, likely lapis lazuli in OT contexts.
roots_lines: Greek sappheiros (G4552) — sapphire; second foundation stone of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19)
Hebrew sappir (H5601) — sapphire; under God's feet at Sinai (Exod 24:10), throne in Ezekiel's vision (Ezek 1:26)
Likely identification: lapis lazuli (deep blue, opaque, with golden pyrite flecks) — the cobalt-blue "stone of heaven" of the ancient Near East
Second of the twelve stones; counterpart to jasper above it and chalcedony below it in the New Jerusalem foundation
usage: Under the God of Sinai was paved sapphire; over our redeemed city, sapphire becomes the second stone we stand upon.
Ezekiel saw sapphire shaped into a throne; John saw sapphire shaped into a foundation — the same stone, the same God, the same line of glory.
Sapphire is not a status symbol; it is the color of the floor of heaven.

etymology: Greek chalkēdōn (G5472) — a cryptocrystalline form of quartz, generally milky white or pale blue; the third foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19). Named after Chalcedon, a city in Asia Minor (modern-day Kadıköy across the Bosphorus from Istanbul) famous for the AD 451 ecumenical council that defined the two-natures Christology that the Reformed tradition still confesses.
biblical_def: Chalcedony is mentioned only once in Scripture: as the third foundation stone of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19). But the name carries a significance the Holy Spirit could not have intended in AD 95 when John wrote — the city of Chalcedon, after which the stone is named, would become four centuries later (AD 451) the site of the Fourth Ecumenical Council that defined the orthodox Christology the Church has confessed ever since: that Jesus Christ is one Person in two natures, fully God and fully man, the two natures "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation," each retaining its own properties yet united in the one Person of the Son. Without this Chalcedonian definition there is no orthodox gospel — for if Christ is not truly God He cannot save, and if He is not truly man He cannot represent us before the Father. The stone itself is a pale, semi-translucent quartz; it shows two-natures-in-one-stone in its layered milky-blue appearance — a happy providential picture of the doctrine that bears its city's name. In the New Jerusalem, chalcedony sits between sapphire (heaven's floor) and emerald (the rainbow of mercy around the throne, Rev 4:3), exactly where the God-Man stands in the order of redemption: between the God of unapproachable glory above and the covenant mercy that brings sinners home.
webster_summary: A pale, translucent quartz; the third foundation of the New Jerusalem and the namesake of the city where the Church defined the two natures of Christ.
webster_full: CHALCEDONY, noun. A whitish or pale blue translucent variety of quartz, with a wax-like luster. Used in ancient seals and cameos.

In Scripture, mentioned only at Rev 21:19 as the third foundation stone of the New Jerusalem. Named after Chalcedon, an ancient city in Bithynia (Asia Minor) — also the site of the Fourth Ecumenical Council (AD 451) that defined the orthodox doctrine of the two natures of Christ.
scriptures: Revelation 21:19
And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, a chalcedony; the fourth, an emerald.
Revelation 21:14
And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
John 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Philippians 2:6-7
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men.
corruption_summary: Chalcedony is corrupted when the doctrine that bears its city's name is softened (one-nature Christologies of every variety) or when the New Jerusalem stones are dismissed as decorative trivia rather than divinely-ordered witness.
corruption_paragraphs: The Christology side. Modern "progressive" theology often softens Chalcedon — speaking of Jesus as "the human face of God" (Spong) or as a uniquely God-conscious man (Schleiermacher) or as God-becoming-in-history (process theology) — all of which violate the careful Chalcedonian fences: without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. To weaken Chalcedon is to lose either a true God who saves or a true Man who represents us. The Reformed confessions (Belgic 19; WCF 8.2; LBCF 8.2) all explicitly reaffirm the Chalcedonian definition because the gospel hinges on it.

The hermeneutics side. Some commentators wave away the New Jerusalem stones as numerological flourish or mere borrowing from Greek precious-stone catalogs. But the Holy Spirit chose twelve stones in a specific order, and the Church has long heard echoes — chalcedony's name later became attached to the city where the Church's confession of the very King who reigns from this New Jerusalem was hammered out. Whether or not John foresaw this providential pun, the Church may rightly receive it as a fitting providence of God.
roots_summary: Greek chalkēdōn (G5472) — a pale, layered, semi-translucent quartz; named for the city of Chalcedon in ancient Bithynia.
roots_lines: Greek chalkēdōn (G5472) — chalcedony; appears only at Rev 21:19, the third foundation stone of the New Jerusalem
Named for Chalcedon, an ancient Bithynian city (modern Kadıköy, Turkey) on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus
Same city hosted the Fourth Ecumenical Council (AD 451), which defined the orthodox doctrine of Christ's two natures in one Person
The stone's two-tone layered appearance is a happy picture of the doctrine: two natures, one Person, undivided yet unconfused
usage: The third stone of the city wall bears the name of the city where the Church confessed Jesus as true God and true Man.
Chalcedony is the gem that quietly preaches Chalcedonian Christology to anyone with ears to hear.
If you reject Chalcedon's two-natures definition, you have rejected the gospel — even if you keep the gem.

etymology: Greek smaragdos (G4665), Hebrew nophek (H5306) or bareketh (H1304) — a brilliant green beryl gem; the fourth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19) and the color of the rainbow around God's throne (Rev 4:3). Some Hebrew sources translate nophek as emerald and others as carbuncle/turquoise; the LXX consistently uses smaragdos.
biblical_def: Emerald is the fourth stone in the foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19) and — most strikingly — the color of the rainbow surrounding the throne of God in John's heavenly vision: "and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald" (Rev 4:3). A rainbow first appears in Scripture as the covenant sign God gave Noah after the flood — His sworn pledge never again to destroy the earth by water (Gen 9:13-17). That seven-color rainbow becomes a single-color green rainbow around the heavenly throne — covenant mercy distilled, the green of life, of the resurrection morning, of the cedars and palms of paradise. Emerald also appears on the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18, third stone in some orderings; some translate as carbuncle), and in Ezekiel's catalog of Eden's stones covering the anointed cherub (Ezek 28:13). The theological line is clear: from Eden's lost paradise (Ezek 28:13) → through the breastplate's representation of God's covenant people (Exod 28) → through Noah's rainbow pledge (Gen 9) → to the emerald rainbow encircling the throne in heaven (Rev 4:3) → to emerald laid as the fourth foundation of the eternal city (Rev 21:19). Green is the color of God's covenant keeping: every place He has sworn He will be merciful, He has marked with this stone or this color. The Father's throne is fenced not with the wrath rainbow only but with the GREEN rainbow — mercy is the dominant note of the eternal court.
webster_summary: A precious green gem, fourth foundation of the New Jerusalem and the emerald rainbow of mercy around God's throne.
webster_full: EMERALD, noun. A precious stone of the beryl family, of a rich green color, valued for its deep transparency.

In Scripture, the fourth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19); the color of the rainbow surrounding the heavenly throne (Rev 4:3); a stone on the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18; though some translate as carbuncle); a stone covering the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13).
scriptures: Revelation 21:19
And the foundations of the wall of the city were garnished with all manner of precious stones. The first foundation was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, a chalcedony; the fourth, an emerald.
Revelation 4:3
And he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.
Genesis 9:13
I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
Ezekiel 28:13

Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God; every precious stone was thy covering, the sardius, topaz, and the diamond, the beryl, the onyx, and the jasper, the sapphire, the emerald, and the carbuncle, and gold.
corruption_summary: Emerald is corrupted when the throne-rainbow of Revelation 4:3 is read as random imagery rather than as covenant mercy intentionally encircling the seat of God's judgments.
corruption_paragraphs: Decoration-only reading. Some commentaries treat the green rainbow around God's throne as poetic flourish — as if the Spirit just thought it would be pretty. But John has told us the throne is the seat from which the seven seal judgments, seven trumpets, seven bowls, and the final assize will issue. Around THAT throne — the throne from which the world's wrath flows — God has placed an emerald rainbow: a green-distilled echo of His covenant pledge to Noah. Mercy is the perimeter of His justice. Every act of judgment proceeds from within an enclosure of pledged grace. Lose this and you read Revelation as raw wrath; keep it and you read Revelation as wrath bounded by covenant.

New Age commodification. As with sapphire and jasper, emerald in much of modern popular spirituality has become a "heart chakra" stone, a vehicle for "unconditional love" energy, etc. The Bible's emerald is not a generator of love-energy; it is the visible token that the God who sits in judgment has already pledged Himself in mercy. Healing crystal merchants strip the gem from its covenant context; recover the covenant and the gem recovers its glory.
roots_summary: Greek smaragdos (G4665), Hebrew nophek (H5306) or bareketh (H1304) — a brilliant green beryl gem; the throne-rainbow color.
roots_lines: Greek smaragdos (G4665) — emerald; fourth foundation of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:19), color of throne-rainbow (Rev 4:3)
Hebrew nophek (H5306) — possibly emerald; on the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:18) and Eden's stones (Ezek 28:13)
Hebrew bareketh (H1304) — sometimes translated emerald or carbuncle; third stone of the breastplate (Exod 28:17)
Green is the biblical color of life and of God's covenant mercy distilled — every emerald reference echoes Noah's rainbow
usage: Around the throne of judgment God has hung an emerald rainbow — His wrath is fenced with His covenant mercy.
The fourth foundation of the eternal city is emerald, and its echo is green: every promise God has kept, every breath of grace held back judgment.
The high priest carried an emerald on his chest as he entered the holy place — covenant mercy worn over the heart.

etymology: Greek sardonux (G4557) — a banded layered variety of onyx, alternating reddish-brown (sardius) layers with white (onyx) layers; the fifth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). Named by combining sardios (the red layer) and onyx (the white layer).
biblical_def: Sardonyx is mentioned only at Revelation 21:20 as the fifth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem. The stone is a banded onyx in which warm red-brown layers alternate with cool white layers — the two colors of blood and bone, of wound and resurrection, set in the same stone by the hand of the Creator. The two foundational onyx stones in the OT priesthood (Exod 28:9-12) bore the names of the twelve tribes engraved on the high priest's shoulders — six names on each — so that he carried the people of God on his shoulders as he entered the holy place to intercede. When the eternal city's foundations bring sardonyx into view, the typological echo is rich: the high priest who once bore the twelve tribes on engraved onyx now reigns as the King-Priest of a city whose foundations bear the names of the twelve apostles (Rev 21:14); blood (sardius/red) and bone-white (onyx) are bound together in a single stone, as the gospel binds together the crucified body and the risen body of the same Christ. The Holy Spirit did not choose plain onyx for the fifth foundation, nor plain sardius for the sixth (which IS the sixth); He chose the BANDED stone where the two colors run together — the stone in which death and life meet in the same mineral fabric. The fifth foundation is a witness in stone to the gospel itself.
webster_summary: A banded onyx with alternating red-brown and white layers; the fifth foundation of the New Jerusalem.
webster_full: SARDONYX, noun. A precious stone of the onyx family, formed of alternating layers of white chalcedony and reddish-brown sard (carnelian). Used in ancient cameos and seals.

In Scripture, mentioned only at Rev 21:20 as the fifth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem. Combines the imagery of two stones — sardius (red, blood) and onyx (white, used on the high priest's shoulder-stones bearing the names of Israel's tribes).
scriptures: Revelation 21:20
The fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst.
Exodus 28:9-10

And thou shalt take two onyx stones, and grave on them the names of the children of Israel: Six of their names on one stone, and the other six names of the rest on the other stone, according to their birth.
Exodus 28:12

And thou shalt put the two stones upon the shoulders of the ephod for stones of memorial unto the children of Israel: and Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial.
Revelation 21:14
And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.
corruption_summary: Sardonyx is corrupted when the layered red-and-white symbolism is missed (treating it as decorative variety) or when the OT onyx-shoulder-stones connection is severed from the NT Lamb who bears the names of His people forever.
corruption_paragraphs: Symbolic flattening. The ancient world had hundreds of precious stones to choose from. The Holy Spirit chose specifically the BANDED stone where red and white meet — sardonyx — for the fifth foundation. Read this stone as mere variety in the catalog and you've missed the typological richness: blood and white-as-snow are bound together in one stone, just as the crucified and risen Christ is one Lord.

Severance from the shoulder-stones. Modern commentaries often discuss the New Jerusalem stones without referencing the high priest's shoulder onyx stones (Exod 28:9-12) on which the names of the twelve tribes were engraved. But the foundations of the city explicitly bear the names of the twelve apostles (Rev 21:14) — the same shoulder-bearing function transposed from priest to city. Sardonyx, which incorporates the onyx of the high priest's shoulders, sits at exactly this typological hinge: the priest who once carried God's people on engraved stones now reigns as the King-Priest of a city whose stones carry the names of those who carried His gospel.
roots_summary: Greek sardonux (G4557) — a banded onyx of red-brown and white layers; the fifth foundation of the New Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Greek sardonux (G4557) — sardonyx; appears only at Rev 21:20, the fifth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem
Compound word: sardios (red-brown carnelian) + onux (white onyx) — the red and white bands fused in one stone
Echoes the two onyx shoulder-stones of the high priest (Exod 28:9-12), engraved with the twelve tribes
Sits beside sardius (the sixth) — the Spirit pairs them deliberately, blood-and-bone-white as the gospel's signature
usage: The fifth foundation is sardonyx — blood-red and bone-white bound in one stone, the gospel pictured in mineral.
What the high priest once carried on his shoulders, the King-Priest now lays as foundation: His people are not borne for a day but built in forever.
Sardonyx is the cross and the empty tomb fused in a single piece of quartz.

etymology: Greek sardios (G4556), Hebrew odem (H124) — a deep blood-red precious stone, identified today as carnelian or red jasper; the sixth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). The stone is named after Sardis, the city in Asia Minor (one of the seven churches of Asia, Rev 3:1-6) where rich deposits of the stone were mined.
biblical_def: Sardius is the sixth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20), the first stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:17; 39:10), one of the precious stones covering the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13), and — most weighty of all — the first half of the appearance of God Himself on the throne in John's vision: "He that sat was to look upon LIKE A JASPER AND A SARDINE STONE" (Rev 4:3). The deep blood-red of sardius pictures the wrath and judgment of God; sardius first, then jasper (clear glory) — but the order in Revelation 4:3 may be deliberate: God's throne appears red-and-clear together, judgment glowing through holiness. The OT breastplate carried sardius as the FIRST stone — the first tribe in the priestly order (Reuben in most reconstructions) — pictured by the stone that represents the cost of approach to God. The New Jerusalem's sixth foundation is the same stone: the city stands on twelve foundations, and the SIXTH is sardius — the stone whose color is the color of blood. Without the blood of the Lamb (Rev 5:9; 7:14), there is no city. The same red-stone that named the church of Sardis ("thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead" — Rev 3:1) preaches a warning: even the city named for the blood-red stone can be dead if her people do not actually drink the blood of Christ. Sardius is the stone of Christ's blood — and that blood is either a foundation or a witness against you.
webster_summary: A deep red precious stone (carnelian); sixth foundation of the New Jerusalem and the red half of God's appearance on the throne.
webster_full: SARDIUS, noun. A precious stone of a deep red color, identified today as carnelian or red jasper. Named after Sardis in Asia Minor where it was anciently mined.

In Scripture, the sixth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20); the first stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:17); a stone covering the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13); the red half of the appearance of God on the throne (Rev 4:3).
scriptures: Revelation 21:20
The fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite.
Revelation 4:3
And he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and there was a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald.
Exodus 28:17
And thou shalt set in it settings of stones, even four rows of stones: the first row shall be a sardius, a topaz, and a carbuncle: this shall be the first row.
Ezekiel 28:13
Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God; every precious stone was thy covering, the sardius, topaz, and the diamond, the beryl, the onyx, and the jasper.
corruption_summary: Sardius is corrupted when the blood-red theology of the stone is stripped (its connection to atonement and wrath dissolved into mere color choice), or when modern commentaries detach Revelation 4:3 from its OT roots in priestly representation.
corruption_paragraphs: Atonement-shy theology. The blood-red of sardius testifies to the price of approach to God. Modern liberal theology, allergic to substitutionary atonement, often refuses to read color symbolism in Scripture this way — preferring abstract "love" or "presence" categories. But the priest carried sardius FIRST, before all other stones, when he approached the holy place. The stone preaches: approach to God is purchased in blood. To remove that is to remove the gospel.

On the other side, some treat sardius and the other stones as raw decorative inventory rather than as theologically loaded. The biblical stones are NOT neutral. Each was chosen, ordered, and placed by the Spirit. Sardius opens the high priest's breastplate; sardius half-defines the appearance of God on the throne; sardius founds the sixth course of the eternal city. Three places in canon — and all three carry the weight of red, blood, and approach. To shrug at this is to read a flatter Bible than the one God wrote.
roots_summary: Greek sardios (G4556), Hebrew odem (H124) — a deep blood-red carnelian or red jasper; named for Sardis in Asia Minor.
roots_lines: Greek sardios (G4556) — sardius/sardine stone; sixth foundation of New Jerusalem, red half of God's appearance (Rev 4:3)
Hebrew odem (H124) — sardius; from adam (red, ground) — same root as the name Adam, the red-earth man
Named for Sardis in Asia Minor (one of the seven churches, Rev 3:1) where the stone was mined
Likely modern equivalent: carnelian or red jasper; the deep-red translucent variety
usage: The sixth foundation is sardius — the blood-red stone, the price of every step into God's city.
On God's throne shines sardius and jasper: justice and glory, wrath and light, never separated.
The high priest entered the holy place wearing sardius first — no approach to God without the cost the stone foretells.

etymology: Greek chrysolithos (G5555) — literally "gold-stone," a yellow-green gem identified today as peridot (gem-quality olivine) or topaz; the seventh foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). Compound of chrysos (gold) + lithos (stone).
biblical_def: Chrysolite is the seventh foundation stone of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). The Greek name chrysolithos means simply "gold-stone" — a yellow-green gem most likely identified today as peridot (gem-quality olivine) mined in antiquity from Zabargad Island in the Red Sea. The number SEVEN is the biblical number of completion and divine perfection (seven days of creation; seven feasts of Israel; seven churches, seals, trumpets, bowls of Revelation; seven Spirits of God before the throne; the seventh stone is therefore the stone of the completion of the city's foundation as a divine work). The OT background is Daniel 10:5-6: in Daniel's vision of a man clothed in linen "his body also was like the beryl" — but the LXX uses chrysolithos here, and many translations render "body like the chrysolite," indicating the gem was associated with the visible appearance of a glorious heavenly being. Ezekiel sees the wheels of the cherubim in his vision as "the colour of a beryl stone" (Ezek 1:16; 10:9), again with chrysolite in some renderings. The seventh foundation being chrysolite carries weight: at the midpoint of the twelve stones, the Spirit places a stone whose name means "gold-stone" and whose color flickers between green (life) and gold (kingdom). The city is golden underfoot (Rev 21:18, 21) and the seventh stone of the foundation is golden through-and-through.
webster_summary: A yellow-green gem (peridot); the seventh foundation stone of the New Jerusalem.
webster_full: CHRYSOLITE, noun. A yellow-green precious stone, identified today as gem-quality olivine (peridot) or sometimes as topaz. The Greek name means literally "gold-stone."

In Scripture, the seventh foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20); possibly the stone described in the body of the heavenly man in Daniel 10:6 (LXX); possibly the color of the cherubic wheels in Ezekiel 1:16 (LXX).
scriptures: Revelation 21:20
The fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus.
Daniel 10:6
His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass.
Ezekiel 1:16
The appearance of the wheels and their work was like unto the colour of a beryl: and they four had one likeness.
Ezekiel 10:9
And when I looked, behold the four wheels by the cherubims, one wheel by one cherub, and another wheel by another cherub: and the appearance of the wheels was as the colour of a beryl stone.
corruption_summary: Chrysolite is corrupted when its position as the seventh stone (the number of divine completion) is dismissed as coincidence, or when the OT connections to the appearance of glorious heavenly beings (Daniel 10, Ezekiel 1) are severed from the NT city's foundation imagery.
corruption_paragraphs: Numerical dismissal. Revelation arranges things in sevens with relentless intentionality: seven churches, seven seals, seven trumpets, seven bowls, seven Spirits, seven thunders. To then treat the seventh foundation stone — chrysolite — as random placement in the catalog is to miss the Spirit's hand. The seventh stone of a list of twelve stones in the book of Revelation is not accident. The position itself preaches: divine completion stands at the midpoint of the city's foundation, gold-named, gold-colored, integral to the structure.

Severance from theophany. The Hebrew of Daniel 10:6 and Ezekiel 1:16 hovers between "beryl" and "chrysolite" in translation, but both visions involve a glorious heavenly being whose body or appearance is described in terms of this gem. Modern commentaries that strip the New Jerusalem stones from their OT theophany contexts lose the chain: chrysolite, the gold-stone, has appeared before in the body of a heavenly messenger and in the wheels of the chariot of God. It is not random that the same Spirit names it again as a foundation of the city where God dwells with man.
roots_summary: Greek chrysolithos (G5555) — literally "gold-stone," a yellow-green gem (likely peridot/olivine); seventh foundation of the New Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Greek chrysolithos (G5555) — chrysolite; from chrysos (gold) + lithos (stone)
Seventh foundation stone of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20) — the stone at the midpoint of the twelve, position of divine completion
Likely modern equivalent: peridot (gem-quality olivine), a yellow-green silicate; anciently mined from Zabargad Island in the Red Sea
Possibly the body-color of the heavenly man in Daniel 10:6 (LXX) and the wheel-color of Ezekiel's cherubim (1:16; 10:9)
usage: The seventh foundation is chrysolite — the gold-stone at the midpoint of the city, divine completion in mineral.
Daniel saw a heavenly man whose body shone like chrysolite; John saw chrysolite laid into the foundation of the city where that Man reigns.
Gold-named, green-colored: chrysolite blends kingdom-gold and resurrection-green in one stone.

etymology: Greek bēryllos (G969), Hebrew tarshish (H8658) — the parent mineral of emerald (green beryl) and aquamarine (pale blue beryl); the eighth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). The Hebrew tarshish may indicate the stone came from Tarshish (the Phoenician trading colony likely in southern Spain).
biblical_def: Beryl is the eighth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20), and the eighth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:20; 39:13) — representing the tribe of Asher in traditional reconstructions. The same Greek word bēryllos appears in Daniel 10:6 ("his body also was like the beryl") describing the glorious heavenly being who appeared to Daniel; in Ezekiel 1:16 and 10:9 the wheels of the cherubim are described as "the colour of a beryl stone" — most likely a pale blue-green sparkling stone. Modern beryl is the parent mineral of emerald (green beryl) and aquamarine (pale blue beryl), with morganite, heliodor, and other varieties. The Hebrew tarshish (H8658) is also the name of a place — most likely the Phoenician trading colony at Tartessos in southern Spain — from which Solomon's fleet brought back precious goods (1 Kings 10:22). The connection between the place name and the stone name suggests the stone came in trade from Tarshish to Israel. Theological weight: the eighth foundation. Eight in Scripture is the number of new beginning (the eighth day of circumcision, Lev 12:3; eight souls saved in the ark, 1 Pet 3:20; eight names of the resurrection day in Christian tradition). The eighth foundation is beryl — the stone of new beginning laid into the city where God begins eternity with His redeemed.
webster_summary: A pale blue-green gem (parent of emerald and aquamarine); the eighth foundation of the New Jerusalem.
webster_full: BERYL, noun. A precious stone, the parent mineral of emerald (green variety) and aquamarine (blue variety). Generally pale blue-green to pale green, sometimes colorless or pink.

In Scripture, the eighth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20); the eighth stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:20); the body-color of the heavenly man in Daniel 10:6; the wheel-color of Ezekiel's cherubim (1:16, 10:9).
scriptures: Revelation 21:20
The seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus.
Daniel 10:6
His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire.
Exodus 28:20
And the fourth row a beryl, and an onyx, and a jasper: they shall be set in gold in their inclosings.
Ezekiel 1:16
The appearance of the wheels and their work was like unto the colour of a beryl: and they four had one likeness.
corruption_summary: Beryl is corrupted when modern translations confuse the gem family (treating beryl, aquamarine, and emerald as unrelated stones) or when the Daniel 10 / Ezekiel 1 theophany contexts are detached from the eternal city's foundation imagery.
corruption_paragraphs: Translation drift. The Hebrew tarshish is sometimes rendered "beryl," sometimes "chrysolite," sometimes "topaz" depending on the version — and modern jewelry treats beryl as its own niche gem distinct from emerald and aquamarine, when in fact they are all the same parent mineral colored by trace elements. The biblical stones were not always strictly identified with modern crystallography; what matters is the Spirit's selection of the stone and the chain of contexts in which it appears across canon.

Theophany context lost. Daniel 10:5-6 describes a glorious heavenly being whose body "was like the beryl" — most readers move on. But the same Greek word for that body's appearance is the same word used for the eighth foundation of the New Jerusalem and for the wheels of the chariot of God in Ezekiel. The pattern is unmistakable: where God appears in glorious vision (and where the city of God is laid in foundation), beryl marks the place. To strip the Daniel-Ezekiel-Revelation connection is to miss the Spirit's deliberate cross-referencing across centuries of Scripture.
roots_summary: Greek bēryllos (G969), Hebrew tarshish (H8658) — a pale blue-green gem, parent mineral of emerald and aquamarine.
roots_lines: Greek bēryllos (G969) — beryl; eighth foundation of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20)
Hebrew tarshish (H8658) — beryl; on the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:20), and possibly named for trade origin in Tartessos (Spain)
Parent mineral of emerald (green), aquamarine (blue), morganite (pink), and heliodor (yellow); colored by trace iron, manganese, etc.
Body of the glorious heavenly man in Daniel 10:6; wheel-color of the cherubic chariot in Ezekiel 1:16 and 10:9
usage: The eighth foundation is beryl — eighth, the number of new beginnings, the stone of the city where God begins again with His redeemed.
Daniel saw a heavenly man whose body shone like beryl; Ezekiel saw God's chariot wheels colored like beryl; John saw beryl laid in the city of God.
Emerald is green beryl; aquamarine is blue beryl — the stone family that crowns Scripture's vision of God's glory.

etymology: Greek topazion (G5116), Hebrew pitdah (H6357) — a precious stone, anciently associated with the yellow-gold or greenish-yellow stones (most likely chrysoberyl or peridot rather than the modern silicate gem); the ninth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). Likely named for Topazos Island in the Red Sea (modern Zabargad).
biblical_def: Topaz is the ninth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20), the second stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:17; 39:10) — representing Simeon in traditional reconstructions — and one of the precious stones covering the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13). The ancient "topaz" was probably not the modern aluminum silicate sold by jewelers today but rather chrysoberyl or peridot — a golden-yellow to yellow-green stone. Job mentions it: "The topaz of Ethiopia shall not equal it [wisdom], neither shall it be valued with pure gold" (Job 28:19) — making topaz a benchmark of preciousness against which divine wisdom is measured (and exceeds). The ninth foundation: nine in Scripture is sometimes associated with finality of judgment (Christ died on the ninth hour, Matt 27:46; the fruit of the Spirit is nine-fold, Gal 5:22-23). In the breastplate it stood beside sardius (blood-red, first) and carbuncle (deep red, third) — a yellow-gold flame between two reds, a small picture of light burning between two judgments. In the eternal city it sits between chrysoprasus (the tenth, pale green) and beryl (the eighth, blue-green) — gold between two greens, like the lamp of God between olive trees (Zech 4). The wisdom that topaz signified for Job has reached its terminus in the city built on the Wisdom Himself, Christ (1 Cor 1:30; Col 2:3).
webster_summary: A yellow-gold precious stone; the ninth foundation of the New Jerusalem and the second stone of the high priest's breastplate.
webster_full: TOPAZ, noun. A precious stone of various colors but most commonly yellow-gold; modern topaz is an aluminum fluorosilicate, but ancient "topaz" was likely chrysoberyl or peridot — a yellow-green stone.

In Scripture, the ninth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20); the second stone of the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:17); one of the precious stones covering the anointed cherub in Eden (Ezek 28:13); a stone against which divine wisdom is measured and exceeds (Job 28:19).
scriptures: Revelation 21:20
The eighth, beryl; the ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst.
Exodus 28:17
And thou shalt set in it settings of stones, even four rows of stones: the first row shall be a sardius, a topaz, and a carbuncle: this shall be the first row.
The topaz of Ethiopia shall not equal it, neither shall it be valued with pure gold.
Ezekiel 28:13
Thou hast been in Eden the garden of God; every precious stone was thy covering, the sardius, topaz, and the diamond.
corruption_summary: Topaz is corrupted when the wisdom-context of Job 28 is severed from the eternal-city context of Revelation 21 (the same stone tying wisdom to the city built on Christ-the-Wisdom), or when modern gem-identification confusion masks the canonical typology.
corruption_paragraphs: Wisdom-and-city severance. Job 28 — the great wisdom chapter — uses topaz as the benchmark of human-attainable preciousness against which the unattainable preciousness of divine wisdom is contrasted: even topaz cannot equal wisdom. When we then encounter topaz as a foundation of the New Jerusalem, the chain is irresistible: the wisdom Job sought is now built INTO the foundation of the eternal city, because Christ — "who is made unto us wisdom" (1 Cor 1:30) — is the cornerstone (Eph 2:20) of that city. To read either passage in isolation is to miss the canonical arc.

Gem-identification confusion. Many translations render Hebrew pitdah as topaz but acknowledge in margin notes that the ancient stone was probably what we call peridot or chrysoberyl today, not modern topaz. Don't let this confuse the theology — the Holy Spirit is naming a stone that ancient hearers would recognize, and the SAME stone appears across breastplate, Eden, Job, and the eternal city. Modern crystallography is irrelevant to the canonical pattern.
roots_summary: Greek topazion (G5116), Hebrew pitdah (H6357) — a precious yellow-gold or yellow-green stone, probably chrysoberyl or peridot in ancient identification.
roots_lines: Greek topazion (G5116) — topaz; ninth foundation stone of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20)
Hebrew pitdah (H6357) — topaz; on the high priest's breastplate (Exod 28:17), Eden's stones (Ezek 28:13), Job's wisdom-comparison (Job 28:19)
Likely named for Topazos Island in the Red Sea (modern Zabargad, Egypt) where the stone was anciently mined
Ancient "topaz" was probably what we now call peridot or chrysoberyl — yellow-green, not the modern aluminum silicate
usage: The ninth foundation is topaz — the stone Job said could not equal wisdom, now built into the city of the Wisdom of God.
On the high priest's breastplate topaz burned beside the reds — a flame of gold between two judgments, mediation in mineral.
Topaz proves that the stones Job longed for outside the city are laid as the foundations within.

etymology: Greek chrysoprasos (G5556) — literally "gold-leek," an apple-green to leek-green variety of chalcedony colored by trace nickel; the tenth foundation of the New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20). Compound of chrysos (gold) + prason (leek).
biblical_def: Chrysoprasus appears only at Revelation 21:20 as the tenth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem. The Greek name chrysoprasos combines chrysos (gold) and prason (leek) — "gold-leek" — describing the stone's pale yellow-green color, like a young leek shoot or apple flesh. Modern chrysoprase is a translucent variety of chalcedony (microcrystalline quartz) colored by trace nickel; it is sometimes called the "stone of Venus" in occult circles but its place in Scripture is purely as one of the twelve named foundation stones. The number ten in Scripture is the number of human completion or ordering (ten commandments; ten plagues on Egypt; ten cities of the Decapolis; the tithe). The tenth foundation, chrysoprasus, sits at the position of human-side completion — and the city's foundation is complete because God Himself has chosen and laid every stone. Three of the twelve stones share the chrysos root: chrysolite (gold-stone, the seventh), chrysoprasus (gold-leek, the tenth), and the city itself is golden (Rev 21:18, 21). The Holy Spirit has woven gold into the foundation of the city not by accident but to signal that the city is treasure — and that even its mineral catalog points to the One who is the treasure hidden in the field (Matt 13:44).
webster_summary: An apple-green chalcedony; the tenth foundation of the New Jerusalem.
webster_full: CHRYSOPRASUS, noun. A pale apple-green or leek-green variety of chalcedony, colored by trace nickel. The Greek name means "gold-leek."
In Scripture, mentioned only at Rev 21:20 as the tenth foundation stone of the New Jerusalem. Modern spelling is also "chrysoprase."
scriptures: Revelation 21:20
The ninth, a topaz; the tenth, a chrysoprasus; the eleventh, a jacinth; the twelfth, an amethyst.
Revelation 21:18
And the building of the wall of it was of jasper: and the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass.
Revelation 21:21
And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.
Matthew 13:44
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.
corruption_summary: Chrysoprasus is corrupted when modern New Age and occult practitioners assign it spiritual properties divorced from God, or when modernist commentary treats it as throwaway color variety rather than as a named, ordered, Spirit-selected stone.
corruption_paragraphs: Occult co-opting. Modern crystal-healing practitioners assign chrysoprase to the heart chakra, to "prosperity," to the "stone of Venus," and to various love-energy uses. The Bible's chrysoprasus is part of the divinely-ordered foundation of the city of God; it has no independent spiritual power. To strip the stone from its biblical context and assign it pagan symbolic functions is precisely the kind of syncretism the Bible repeatedly forbids.

Throwaway-stone reading. The other extreme is to treat chrysoprasus as just another item in a list — one more color in the rainbow of the city's foundations. But the Spirit named twelve specific stones in a specific order. The tenth stone, chrysoprasus, is the second of the three chrysos-named stones (chrysolite, chrysoprasus); it shares a root with the city's golden street and golden walls. The repeated gold theme is not random. The city of God is golden through-and-through — wall, street, foundations — because it is the treasure of which Christ said the kingdom is like.
roots_summary: Greek chrysoprasos (G5556) — literally "gold-leek," an apple-green chalcedony; tenth foundation of the New Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Greek chrysoprasos (G5556) — chrysoprasus; from chrysos (gold) + prason (leek)
Tenth foundation stone of New Jerusalem (Rev 21:20) — the only canonical appearance of the word
Modern equivalent: chrysoprase, a translucent green chalcedony colored by trace nickel; mined today in Australia and Poland
Second of three chrysos-rooted stones in the city's foundation: chrysolite (7th), chrysoprasus (10th); the city itself is golden (Rev 21:18, 21)
usage: The tenth foundation is chrysoprasus — "gold-leek," the pale-green chalcedony that echoes the golden city above it.
Three gold-named stones run through the city's foundation; the city itself is gold; God has built treasure into His treasure.
Don't buy a chrysoprase for the heart chakra; receive the heart-chakra-free Christ who is the actual treasure of the kingdom.
